title: Everything praise (Psalm 148)
hookLine: sun, moon, sea monsters, snow, kings and children, praise
carry: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar

cards: A choir director stands up before the concert and takes the roll. Sopranos? Here.

teach.h: FROM THE HEAVENS: SUN AND MOON
teach.b: The psalm has two halves, like a camera tilting from the sky down to the ground. First the heavens: angels, hosts, and, in the King James Bible, "Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light."

Then, from verse seven, the earth: "Praise the LORD from the earth, ye dragons, and all deeps." Dragons. The Hebrew is tanninim, great sea creatures, the same word Genesis uses for the great sea monsters of the fifth day.
Creatures that frightened the ancient imagination are in the choir.
Then the weather: "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word." A storm here isn't chaos. It's doing what it was told.
Then mountains and fruit trees, beasts and creeping things, and finally people, every rank mixed together: "Both young men, and maidens; old men, and children."

teach.h: KINGS IN THE SAME ROW AS CHILDREN
teach.b: Kings stand in the same row as kids.
Why should a rock or a snowflake praise? One old answer: not with words, but by being what it is. A cedar praises by growing like a cedar.

In the Greek Bible, the book of Daniel includes a long song of three young men in a furnace, calling on everything from frost to whales to bless the Lord; Catholics and Orthodox read it as scripture, and Anglicans sing it as the Benedicite.
And Francis of Assisi wrote his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God through Brother Sun and Sister Moon. The hymn All Creatures of Our God and King comes from it.

how: Psalm 148 is a traditional morning praise psalm in many churches, and it is echoed in the Benedicite canticle and in hymns such as "All Creatures of Our God and King."

o: all creation called to praise, from stars to sea monsters
a promise to thank God for every good thing that happens
praise that only the angels in heaven are able to give

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: in the same row as kings

s: Psalm 148 calls only people to praise
it calls angels, stars, sea monsters, hail, mountains, animals and people.
the psalm's dragons are the same word Genesis uses for great sea creatures
tanninim, made on the fifth day.
in this psalm, the stormy wind is a sign of chaos

games.q: you're writing the guest list for a choir of praise. who makes the psalm's list?
o: angels, sea monsters, hail, cedars, kings and children.
games.why: everything. heaven first, then earth, then every kind of person, old and young, side by side.

practice: Name ten things in creation, slowly, one breath each: the light in the window, a cloud, a crow, a tree you pass every day, rain, your grandmother's hands, a child somewhere laughing, something huge, something tiny.
When you reach ten, sit with the whole crowd of them. If you pray, let each name be a small praise; if not, simply let the list be wonder.

wordCard.voice: Everything praise. Psalm one hundred forty-eight's roll call: angels, stars, sea monsters, hail, cedars, kings and children, all called into one choir.

orig.note: Hebrew: great sea creatures, the King James Bible's dragons. the same word as Genesis 1:21.

carryVoice: Your line: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar. That's one old answer to how a snowflake can praise. See you tomorrow.
